<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Frederica S. Wilson, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes>: INTRODUCTION
H.R. 6502, the College Financial Aid Clarity Act of 2025, would require the Secretary of Education to establish requirements for presenting and formatting financial aid offer letters for institutions of higher education that receive federal financial assistance under the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA). As students decide which institution of higher education is right for them, it is imperative that they have information about the financial aid packages that they are eligible for at each institution. Ideally these financial aid packages would be presented in a format that is standardized, allowing students to easily compare aid packages between institutions. While this bill does add requirements towards the goal of a standardized offer letter, H.R. 6502 falls short of true standardization and overcomplicates the elements necessary to present cost information on financial aid offer letters in a clear and transparent manner. Committee Democrats strongly urge Republicans to make significant changes to this bill prior to its consideration in the House to ensure it substantially improves transparency for students, instead of making them more confused.
CONGRESS NEEDS TO IMPROVE FINANCIAL AID OFFERS
Financial aid offers are provided by institutions of higher education to give admitted students information about the types of aid the school is offering them to defray the cost of their higher education.\1\ Institutions that participate in the student financial assistance programs authorized by the Higher Education Act of 1965 (HEA) are required to disclose information on the cost of attending to students.\2\ However there is no federal law requiring institutions to provide a financial aid offer to accepted students, let alone one in a standardized format with consistent terminology and clarity of information in their financial aid offers.\3\ The lack of standardization and inconsistent presentation of financial aid offers across institutions makes it difficult for students and families to understand and compare cost and aid information. A groundbreaking 2018 report by New America analyzed award letters from over 500 institutions of higher education and found little to no consistency in terms used or how information was presented.\4\ In one of the reports most egregious findings, 455 schools offered unsubsidized student loans, but 136 different terms were used to describe that loan, including 24 who did not even use the word ``loan'' in their term.\5\ It is unsurprising then that students and families face challenges navigating college financial aid offers between institutions because these offers often vary widely.\6\

In addition to using non-standard terminology, award letters vary greatly in the data they provide students to make their decision. In a 2022 report, the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that most colleges and universities do not provide students with all the information necessary to help them clearly understand their financial aid offers.\7\ GAO reported that approximately 55% of institutions do not provide a total cost of attendance data point, one that reflects both direct and indirect costs for students.\8\ GAO also found that an estimated 91% of institutions either do not include or understate the net price\9\ in their financial aid offers.\10\ As a result of these findings, GAO recommended federal lawmakers to take up legislation to mandate institutions of higher education to follow best practices for providing students with clear and standard financial aid offers.\11\ GAO is not alone in this recommendation. Stakeholders have also urged standardization of financial aid offers to help students and families make better informed decisions about college.\12\
\7\U.S. Gov't Accountability Off., GAO-23-104708, FINANCIAL AID OFFERS Action Needed to Improve Information on College Costs and Student Aid 26, (2022) https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-23-104708.pdf.
\8\Id. at 9. GAO defined direct costs as ``Costs that are typically billed directly by the college. Examples include tuition, fees, and on-campus housing and meals.'' Id. at 6. It defined indirect costs as ``Costs that students pay to other parties throughout the academic term. Examples include books, academic supplies, off-campus housing and meals, and other miscellaneous expenses, such as transportation.'' Id. The sum of these direct and indirect costs as defined by GAO greatly mirrors HEA's cost of attendance.
\9\Id. at 9. GAO defined net price as ``The actual amount a student will need to pay to attend a particular college. This should be estimated by subtracting gift aid (and not loans or work-study) from the full cost of attendance (key direct and indirect costs)''. Id. at 6.
\10\Id. at 9.
\11\Id. at 36.

H.R. 6502 ATTEMPTS TO IMPROVE FINANCIAL AID OFFERS
H.R. 6502 partially addresses the need for standardization and clarity in the financial aid offer letter process. Specifically, the bill would require the Secretary of Education to develop best practices and standards that institutions must adopt in formatting their financial aid offer letters. As part of their financial aid offer, institutions would be required to include two standardized measures of estimated costs to the student for the award year the offer covers. The first, required costs, include tuition, fees, and room and board when the institution requires these services be purchased through the institution. The second cost metric institutions would be required to provide students is the total cost of attendance, the sum of the required costs and other costs such as transportation, books, and supplies not typically billed directly by the institution.
H.R. 6502 would also require offer letters to list any grants and scholarships awarded to the student both for the award year the offer covers, and total length of the student's program of study. The bill mandates inclusion of loan information for each loan that a student is eligible for, and student employment options (e.g., federal work-study or state work-study programs). As most students now view their offer letters online, the bill requires the letters to include a link to the universal net price calculator to help students and families compare college costs across institutions. Finally, the bill requires financial aid offer letters to also include four program-level cost metrics based on information from the most recent award year: (1) average annual net price required for completion, (2) total average net price required for completion, (3) average annual price of attendance, and (4) total average annual net price of attendance.
The requirements in H.R. 6502 represent an effort to bring some transparency into college costs and financial aid. By requiring institutions to present information on the cost of attendance, net price, itemized information on grants and scholarships, loans, and work-study using consistent formatting requirements, this bill would mandate some clarity and standardization where none currently exists. However, the bill does not go far enough in terms of standardization to be the true tool students and their families could rely on to make their college decisions. Conversely, the bill arguably adds too many data points of dubious value to the letter. The result is a bill that sews as much confusion in the offer letter process as it attempts to remove with standardization.
H.R. 6502 CREATES MORE CONFUSION IN EXAMINING AND COMPARING FINANCIAL
AID OFFERS
H.R. 6502 falls short of providing uniform financial aid offers across institutions. While the bill requires specific formatting requirements, it simultaneously allows for variations in how institutions lay out and design their financial aid offers, variation we know already creates confusion when students compare aid offers.\13\ Unfortunately, despite the bill's standardization requirements, H.R. 6502 does not solve the problem that colleges and universities display financial aid offers in different ways, which will impede students' ability to compare college costs and aid information.\14\
\13\See Burd et al., supra note 3 at 7 (``Without guidelines, like federally-required nutrition labels or the window sticker for car sales, the consumer is left without an apples-to-apples comparison for a major financial decision.''). See Nesbit, supra note 6 (decrying how even with standardized terms non-standardized layout can make comparing offers confusing) (``Create a spreadsheet to compare the net cost of different colleges side by side. Some financial aid letters will make this information easier to find than others. You may have to dig around on the college website.'') (emphasis added).
\14\Id.
In that sense, H.R. 5602 is a revision from the standardization mandate the Majority championed just last year. Since the 116th Congress, there has been bipartisan Committee support for the Understanding the True Cost of College Act, a bill that takes a more proscriptive approach in both the design and requirements of financial aid award letters.\15\ In the 118th Congress, Republicans passed out of Committee the College Cost Reduction Act (CCRA), which incorporated an updated version of the Understanding the True Cost of College Act. This updated version would actually require the Secretary to develop the form schools would use as the basis of their offer letters.\16\ Committee Democrats did not support the passage of CCRA, but in Minority Views accompanying the bill's Committee report expressed support for ``creating a standardized financial aid form to provide students and families with more clarity on college costs.''\17\
